volumes.title: What Hester Left
volumes.text:
When Bram Coddle gave up the Emberwick ferry after forty years, he expected to spend his days sitting down. Then his aunt Hester died, at ninety, and left him her pottery in Kiln Lane: one low shed, one cold kiln, eleven sacks of clay and a kick wheel she had always called Maud.

Bram had never made a pot in his life. He had, however, broken one. On the bench lay Hester’s order book, and its final line, in her square hand, read: One porridge bowl for Bram, who broke his. Not yet begun.

He read it twice, standing among the dust sheets. Then he took off his coat, hung it on the nail where her apron still was, and looked at the wheel. The wheel, it seemed to him, looked back. Neither of them was impressed.

volumes.title: The First Kick
volumes.text:
Bram Coddle, forty years a ferryman, sat down at his late aunt’s kick wheel on a Monday in April, meaning to have a porridge bowl made by dinner time.

The wheel was a heavy thing: a stone flywheel below, a small oak wheelhead above, and an iron spindle between. Hester had called it Maud. Bram set a lump of clay in the middle, wetted his hands as he had seen her do, and kicked. Maud groaned like a gate. She went round nine times, each turn slower and more grudging than the last, and stopped. Bram kicked harder. She managed eleven turns, shuddered, and stopped again, and the clay slid gently off the wheelhead and into his lap.

He sat a while with it there. On the ferry, he reflected, when you pushed a thing, it had at least the manners to move.

volumes.title: Oil and Opinions
volumes.text:
Word went down Kiln Lane that Bram Coddle, the old ferryman, could not make his aunt Hester’s kick wheel go round. By Wednesday he had more advice than clay.

The baker said the floor was out of true. The blacksmith said the spindle wanted replacing and he could do it for nine shillings. Mrs Larkin next door said Hester used to sing to it. Bram tried the cheapest remedy first. He fetched the tub of grease he had used on the ferry winch, and he oiled the spindle top and bottom until it shone like an eel.

Then he kicked. The wheel turned exactly as before: nine sour turns, a shudder, a stop. The only change was the smell, which was now strongly of the river. He did not try singing. A man has his limits, and the window was open.

volumes.title: Levelling the Floor
volumes.text:
The baker had told Bram Coddle that the floor of his late aunt’s pottery sloped, and that this was why her old kick wheel fought him at every turn. Bram, a retired ferryman with time on his hands, set a bowl of water on the wheelhead to see. The water sat as flat as a pond.

He levelled the floor anyway. He spent two days tapping oak wedges under the wheel’s legs, checking the bowl, and tapping again. When he had finished, it was the most level object in Emberwick. He kicked it. Nine turns, a shudder, a stop.

A small girl was watching from the doorway with a basket of eggs. This was Pim Larkin from next door, aged nine. “Miss Hester’s went round for ages,” she said. “It hummed.” Bram thanked her for the eggs and, with great self-control, for the information.

volumes.title: Clay on the Beam
volumes.text:
By May, Bram Coddle had worked out one way to keep his aunt Hester’s stubborn wheel turning: kick it without stopping, hard, like a man running upstairs. This left him no breath and no attention for the clay, but he had been a ferryman, and ferrymen are used to doing two things at once.

On the Thursday he got the wheel going at a furious lick. The clay rose under his hands into something very like a bowl. He had time to feel proud. Then the wheel gave its shudder, and the bowl leaned, let go of the wheelhead altogether, and flew. It struck the roof beam above the door and stayed there.

Bram looked at it for some time. It was, he decided, the best thing he had made so far. He left it on the beam, where it dried, and where it remains.

volumes.title: The Wheelwright Replies
volumes.text:
After two months of being beaten by his late aunt’s kick wheel, Bram Coddle of Kiln Lane swallowed his pride and wrote to the man who had built it: Osric Thane, wheelwright, of Cragfold in the Northern Fells. He described the nine grudging turns, the shudder, the stop. He enclosed a stamp.

The answer came in a week, on the back of a bill for cart spokes. “I made that wheel for Hester Coddle fifty years ago and it has never wanted anything but clay. There is nothing wrong with it. I would look to the kicker.”

Bram read this aloud to the wheel, with feeling. He had carried half of Emberwick across the Ember, in all weathers, without once being told to look to the ferryman. He put the letter on the fire. Then, being honest, he took it off again and kept it.

volumes.title: The Ferryman’s Lean
volumes.text:
Bram Coddle had stood forty years at a ferry pole, and it had left him with a lean: left shoulder down, weight on the right foot, as if the floor might drift. He never noticed it until he took up his late aunt’s pottery. The clay noticed at once.

Everything he coaxed off her stubborn wheel that June leaned the way he did. There was a dish that sloped like a hat brim. There was a pot with one high side, as though it were listening for something. Pim Larkin from next door, who was nine, named them as they came: the Slipper, the Nosy One, the Boat.

Still, they were pots. They held water, mostly. Bram lined them up on the sill beside Hester’s own straight-backed jugs, where they looked like a family in which the good sense had run out early.

volumes.title: Hester’s Clogs
volumes.text:
Sweeping under the bench one wet morning, Bram Coddle found his aunt Hester’s work clogs. She had been the potter of Kiln Lane for fifty years, and he, a retired ferryman, had been failing to work her kick wheel since April.

They were plain alder clogs, grey with clay. The odd thing was the wear. The right one might have been bought last week. The left was worn through at the ball of the foot, right through, with a patch of leather tacked over the hole and a second hole coming in the patch.

Bram turned them over in his hands. Hester had not limped; she had walked into town every market day until she was eighty-eight. He could make nothing of it. He set the clogs side by side under the wheel, since that was plainly where they lived, and went back to his sweeping.

volumes.title: Pim Has a Go
volumes.text:
It rained for three days in July, and Pim Larkin, aged nine, spent them in Bram Coddle’s pottery, watching the old ferryman lose to his late aunt’s kick wheel. On the third day she asked if she could have a go. Bram, who was tired, said she was welcome to it.

Pim’s legs were too short to kick as he did. She wriggled round on the seat, hooked her left foot on the flywheel, and shoved it the only way she could reach, which was backwards.

The wheel did not groan. It went round, and round, and went on going round, with a low steady hum like a kettle thinking about boiling. Pim took her foot away. The wheel spun on by itself. Bram counted sixty turns before he stopped counting and sat down on a sack of clay.

volumes.title: Turning Widdershins
volumes.text:
The trouble with the stubborn wheel in Kiln Lane had been simple all along, and it took a child of nine to find it. Bram Coddle, retired ferryman, had been kicking it the wrong way round.

His aunt Hester was left-footed. For fifty years she had driven that wheel with her left foot, and the iron spindle had worn its seat to suit her, as a path wears to suit one walker. Turned her way, it ran like cream. Turned his, it was a ferry hauled against the current, which is a thing Bram felt he ought to have recognised.

Her worn left clog had told him. The wheelwright’s letter had told him. He spent August learning it all again backwards: left foot, hands changed over, the clay coming at him from the other side. It was like being nine himself, and he found he did not mind.

volumes.title: One Honest Bowl
volumes.text:
In September, Bram Coddle sat down at his late aunt’s kick wheel, set it humming with his left foot the way she had, and made a porridge bowl. It took him the morning. It was thick in the wall and not perfectly round, but it stood up straight, which no pot of his had done before.

The first one cracked across the bottom as it dried. He made it again. The second he glazed brown from Hester’s own bucket and fired in her small kiln, feeding the fire through one long night with Pim Larkin’s father to keep him awake.

When the kiln had cooled he lifted the bowl out into the daylight. There was a small thumbprint baked into the foot, where a nine-year-old had picked it up wet to see underneath. Bram considered it and decided the bowl was the better for a signature.

volumes.title: Entry Closed
volumes.text:
On the first cold morning of October, Bram Coddle made porridge and ate it out of a bowl he had thrown himself, on his aunt Hester’s wheel, in her pottery in Kiln Lane. It had taken a retired ferryman six months, and one small neighbour, to get that far. The porridge tasted much as porridge does. He had a second helping regardless.

Afterwards he washed the bowl, took down Hester’s order book and found her last line: One porridge bowl for Bram, who broke his. Not yet begun. He crossed out the last three words and wrote Delivered, with the date.

Then, since the page had room, he added a line of his own beneath it. One mug for Pim Larkin, with a handle. Begun. Overhead, the bowl that flew off in May kept its place on the roof beam. The wheel hummed. He had left it turning.

volumes.title: A Clean Shed
volumes.text:
Glaze notebook of Wenna Sorrel, potter, Marsh End, Emberwick. Begun the week old Jory Pender retired to the Grey Coast and left me the pottery, the customers, and a glaze shed that had not been tidied since before I was born.

I have tidied it. Forty years of crusted buckets are scrubbed. The battered copper ladle he stirred with, green as a pond and bent like a question mark, I could not quite throw out, so it hangs on a nail by the door. I stir now with a clean beech paddle.

Test 1. Ember green, the glaze everybody wants, from Jory’s own card: wood ash, river clay, sand, patience. Six bowls dipped and fired. They came out brown. Not a bad brown. The brown of good gravy. But I have forty orders for green, and nobody has ever asked me for gravy.

volumes.title: Mustard, and the Twins
volumes.text:
Wenna Sorrel’s glaze notebook, Marsh End pottery. I am trying to make my old master’s Ember green, the green of the river under the willows, and getting brown.

Test 2. More ash, on the theory that Jory Pender never measured anything and had a heavy hand. I burned applewood prunings from the orchard behind the yard and sieved the ash twice. Result: mustard. A cheerful, loud mustard, the colour of a waistcoat at a wedding. Accident: two jugs toppled together in the kiln and fused at the shoulder for good. I have named them the Twins and put them on the high shelf.

I wrote to Jory at Cockle Stairs to ask what I am doing wrong. His postcard came by return, with a picture of a lighthouse. It says, in full: “Can’t think. It was always green for me. Weather fine.”

volumes.title: The Sneeze
volumes.text:
Notebook of Wenna Sorrel, who inherited the Marsh End pottery and cannot make its famous green glaze. Test 3 was meant to be a thicker coat, each mug held under for a slow count of five.

On the count of three I sneezed. It was the ash dust. Six mugs got a double coat on one side, a splash on the other, and a good deal went on my apron. I fired them anyway, since the kiln was going and I dislike waste.

The thick glaze crawled in the heat. It pulled itself up into beads and ridges, glossy and brown-gold, exactly like the back of a toad. They are the ugliest mugs I have ever made. The landlord of the Heron bought all six before they were cool, and wants six more. I have had to write down how I sneezed. Accident named: Toad.

volumes.title: Rain in the Bucket
volumes.text:
I am Wenna Sorrel, potter at Marsh End, and this notebook records my attempts at Ember green, a glaze my master made for forty years and never once wrote down properly.

Test 4 was decided by the roof. A slate slipped in Tuesday’s gale, and by morning the glaze bucket had taken in a good two inches of rain. I had bowls waiting and no time to mix fresh, so I stirred the puddle in and dipped.

Thin glaze makes a thin coat. The bowls came out pale, clear honey, with the red clay glowing through like a hand held up to a candle. Not green. Not within a mile of green. But old Mrs Varley held one up to the window for so long that I gave it to her. Accident named: Weak Tea. The slate is mended. I rather miss the leak.

volumes.title: The Wrong Ash
volumes.text:
Glaze notebook, Marsh End pottery, Wenna Sorrel writing. Still hunting Jory Pender’s Ember green. Still not finding it.

Test 5 was not my idea. I sent the carter’s boy for a sack of applewood ash, and he came back with a sack of something grey and light, which he swore was the same. It was reed ash, from the thatchers burning their trimmings out on the marsh. I found that out after the firing.

The glaze had gone milky and soft, a blue-grey with no shine to it, the colour of the marsh at six in the morning before anything has decided to move. I stood at the kiln door and said nothing for a while. Accident named: Marsh Morning. I paid the boy a penny extra and told him to make the same mistake every month. He is still thinking it over.

volumes.title: Slip’s Walk
volumes.text:
This is the glaze notebook of Wenna Sorrel of Marsh End. The yard cat here is called Slip. She came with the pottery, like the debts.

Test 6: perhaps the secret of Ember green is the water. Jory Pender always said the colour was the river under the willows, so I carried two pails up from the Ember itself, from under the actual willows, and mixed the glaze with that instead of well water. I glazed a dozen tiles and laid them on a board to dry.

Slip crossed the board in the night. Eleven tiles, one paw each, and a pause on the twelfth to wash. The prints fired in perfectly, pale on dark. The glaze was brown, river or no river. But the schoolmistress wants the whole row for her hearth. Accident named: Slip’s Walk. The cat has asked for nothing.

volumes.title: Treacle on the Shelf
volumes.text:
Wenna Sorrel, Marsh End pottery, glaze notebook. Test 7 of my master’s lost green: the same recipe, fired hotter, in case forty years of Jory Pender’s kiln ran fiercer than he knew.

It ran fiercer than I knew. I sat down by the firebox at midnight to rest my eyes, and woke at three with the spy-hole white as the moon. I have never moved so quickly. It was too late for the pots.

The glaze had melted clean off the shoulders and pooled round every foot, thick and dark and glassy. Nine jars were stuck fast to the shelf. I got four off with a chisel and my whole vocabulary. Inside each, where the glaze gathered, is a deep brown pool you could lose a spoon in. Accident named: Treacle. Lesson: a potter may rest her eyes, but only one at a time.

volumes.title: A Visit to the Coast
volumes.text:
I shut the Marsh End pottery for two days and took the carrier’s cart to Cockle Stairs on the Grey Coast, to ask Jory Pender to his face how he made Ember green. Seven tests in this notebook, and I, Wenna Sorrel, have produced every colour but that one.

He was on a bench in his daughter’s garden with a rug over his knees, pleased to see me, and no help. Ash, clay, sand. No, he never weighed it. No, nothing else went in. “Stir it, mind,” he said. “I stirred it every morning for forty years, whether I was glazing or not. A glaze likes to be stirred.”

Test 8, on my return: stirred each morning for two weeks, a hundred turns of the beech paddle, counted. Brown. A beautifully mixed brown. He gave me a bag of shrimps for the journey, which was more use.

volumes.title: The Thrush Bowls
volumes.text:
Glaze notebook of Wenna Sorrel, potter, Marsh End. The shelf of accidents above my bench is filling: the Twins, Toad, Weak Tea, Marsh Morning, Slip’s Walk, Treacle. The space I left for Ember green, my old master’s glaze, is still a space.

Test 9 was spoiled before it began. The blacksmith came to mend the kiln door, and filed a hinge while standing over my open bucket. I saw the dust go in, fine as pepper. I glazed with it out of pure temper.

Every speck of iron bloomed in the fire. The bowls came out cream-brown, freckled all over with dark rust, like a thrush’s breast. The blacksmith says he should have a share. I have offered him a bowl. Accident named: Thrush. I notice I no longer mind these as I should. A person could get fond of being wrong.

volumes.title: The Broken Paddle
volumes.text:
Wenna Sorrel’s glaze notebook, Marsh End pottery, in the tenth month of failing to make Jory Pender’s Ember green.

Accident first, for once. The glaze had settled hard as a brick in the bottom of the bucket, and when I leaned on my beech paddle to shift it, the paddle snapped at the neck. I had nothing else to hand. I took Jory’s old copper ladle down off its nail by the door, bent and green as ever, and stirred with that. Being busy with the autumn fair, I left it standing in the bucket all week.

Test 10 was only meant to use up the batch. But the bowls have come out different. There is a breath of green at the rims, faint as the river in March, where the glaze lies thinnest. I had opened a new sack of sand that week. I have ordered three more.

volumes.title: Two Columns
volumes.text:
I am Wenna Sorrel, potter, and for most of a year this notebook has chased one glaze: Ember green, which my old master made at Marsh End for forty years. Last month, by accident, I got a faint green rim. I thought it was the new sand. Test 11: new sand, mended paddle, everything else the same. Brown.

So I ruled two columns, as my mother did for the housekeeping. Left, the green firing. Right, this one. Ash the same, clay the same, water, sand, heat, all the same. One line was left over, and it was the ladle.

I took it to the window. Outside it is crusted green, but the bowl of it is worn thin as a leaf and scoured bright. Forty years of stirring, and the glaze has been eating it a grain at a time. Jory never added copper. He simply never took it out.

volumes.title: Ember Green
volumes.text:
The last entry in this glaze notebook, kept by Wenna Sorrel at the Marsh End pottery, Emberwick.

Test 12. I stood Jory Pender’s old copper ladle in the bucket and left it there a month, stirring each morning as he did, and going against every tidy instinct I own. Yesterday I opened the kiln. Green. The deep, wet green of the Ember under the willows, pooling darker in the hollows. I sat down on the kiln step. I sent the first bowl to Cockle Stairs, and Jory’s postcard, with a different lighthouse, says: “Told you. Stir it.”

I have added a line to his recipe card: one old ladle, left in. The green has its place on the shelf now, beside Toad and Thrush and Marsh Morning, which I shall go on making. It was the one I looked for. I am not certain it is my favourite.

volumes.title: The Survey Begins
volumes.text:
Being a survey of the domestic jugs of the Lowlands, undertaken for the Emberwick Antiquarian Society by Miss Philippa Quince, Honorary Surveyor, with a donkey cart, a measuring tape and two hundred gummed labels. The donkey is called Bursar. He was the Society’s only other volunteer.

We crossed the Ember at Withy Bridge, where an old woman in a toll-keeper’s coat took my halfpenny and looked at Bursar’s teeth. “Jugs,” she said, when I explained. “You’ll find more jugs than sense down there.” I did not record this as evidence.

Jug No. 1, Sedgeholt, the property of Mrs Annet Fairlock. Height eight inches. Brown glaze, sound, one chip to the lip. Present use: milk. Beneath the handle is a small stamped frog, no larger than a fingernail. A potter’s mark, presumably. I note it for completeness.

volumes.title: Change from a Goose
volumes.text:
The Lowlands survey of jugs, conducted by Miss Philippa Quince for the Emberwick Antiquarian Society, reached Low Marrow on a Thursday. Bursar the donkey reached it some minutes later, having stopped for a hedge.

Jug No. 4, the Plough inn, Low Marrow. Height eleven inches, capacity three pints. Brown glaze, the handle broad and comfortable. Present use: cider. Under the handle, a small stamped frog. That is the second frog in four jugs.

I asked the landlord, Mr Tobias Henge, where the jug was bought. He said it was not bought. His grandfather had it as change. Change from what, I asked. “From a goose,” said Mr Henge, and went to see to the fire. I have written this down exactly as it was said. A surveyor records. She is not required to understand, though I confess I should prefer to.

volumes.title: A Left Thumb
volumes.text:
I am Miss Philippa Quince, surveying the jugs of the Lowlands for the Emberwick Antiquarian Society, and at Cowslip Ending I was shown into the chapel vestry.

Jug No. 9. Height nine inches. Brown glaze, thin at the shoulder. Present use: flowers, on Sundays; the rest of the week it holds the verger’s spectacles. Under the handle, the frog again. That makes five. Whoever makes the frog jugs finishes each handle by pressing a thumb into the clay at its foot. The print is there in every one. I tried my own right thumb in the hollow and it sat wrongly. My left fitted like a key.

So: one potter, left-handed, with a thumb a little broader than mine. The verger asked whether this was important. I said that in a survey everything is important until proved otherwise. Bursar, outside, was eating the chapel’s hollyhocks.

volumes.title: The Oldest Jug of All
volumes.text:
The jug survey of the Lowlands, by Miss Philippa Quince of the Emberwick Antiquarian Society, came to Nine Sluices. The sluice-keeper, Mr Cuthbert Lode, sent word that he owned the oldest jug in the country and I had better bring a cushion to kneel on.

Jug No. 12. Height seven inches. Blue and white. Mr Lode says it is three hundred years old and was dug from the fen by his great-grandfather. On the front, in gold letters, are the words A Present from the Grey Coast. I have entered its age as uncertain.

His wife keeps the dripping in another jug, which he would not have me measure, as it is only the frog one from the bridge road. I measured it while he fetched his great-grandfather’s spade. Nine inches. Frog. Mrs Lode says it has never dripped, which is more than she will say for the sluice.

volumes.title: Sparkle in the Clay
volumes.text:
A trip back to Emberwick for more labels cost me a second halfpenny at Withy Bridge. The old toll-keeper asked how many jugs I had found. Fourteen, I said. “Is that all,” she said, and let Bursar through. I am Miss Philippa Quince, and this is the Antiquarian Society’s survey of Lowland jugs, resumed at Mallowby.

Jug No. 15, the property of the brickmaker, Mr Silas Trow. Height ten inches. Frog under the handle. Present use: none, having lost its base to a frost. That was my luck. In the broken edge the clay shows red, with tiny bright specks that glitter when turned.

Mr Trow knows clay as I know catalogues. No pit in the Lowlands has that sparkle, he says. It is river-bank clay, from up the Ember. I have wrapped a fragment in my handkerchief and labelled it.

volumes.title: The Umbrella Stand
volumes.text:
Survey of the jugs of the Lowlands, for the Emberwick Antiquarian Society. Surveyor, Miss Philippa Quince. Transport, one donkey, Bursar, at his own speed.

Jug No. 22, Hen’s Causeway, the property of the widow Fogg. Height nineteen inches; capacity, by her account, two gallons and a kitten. It is the largest frog jug yet. Present use: umbrellas. Scratched beneath the frog is a wavy line, like water. I have now seen that line on four.

I have formed a theory. So many jugs, over so many years, cannot be one pair of hands. There was once a Frog Pottery: a manufactory of some size, with a dozen workers, a tall chimney, perhaps a wharf. It has been forgotten, and I shall be the one to find it. Mrs Fogg listened to all this very kindly and asked whether I would like a boiled egg.

volumes.title: Eggs and a Favour
volumes.text:
At Otterditch the lane was under four inches of water and Bursar declined it, so I walked the last half mile with the measuring tape round my neck. I am Miss Philippa Quince, and I survey Lowland jugs for the Emberwick Antiquarian Society.

Jug No. 27, the property of Mr Enoch Wherry, eel-catcher. Height eight inches. Frog. It leaks from a crack, and holds nothing, and sits in the middle of his mantelpiece. I asked why he kept it. “It was change,” he said, “from two dozen eggs and a favour.”

That word again. I heard it at Low Marrow, of a goose. I conclude that Change is an old Lowland name for a fair or market, since lost, at which my Frog Pottery sold its wares. I shall propose this to the Society in a footnote. Mr Wherry said I was welcome to propose what I liked.

volumes.title: In Eleven Pieces
volumes.text:
This survey of the jugs of the Lowlands has, until today, damaged nothing. I, Miss Philippa Quince, Honorary Surveyor to the Emberwick Antiquarian Society, must now record otherwise.

At Much Wading the Misses Dabney set out their jugs for me on a table in the yard. I had tied Bursar to the gatepost. I had not tied the gate. He walked in backwards, as donkeys will when a cart is behind them, and the cart met the table.

Jug No. 31. Height formerly six inches. Yellow glaze, no frog. Condition: eleven pieces. Cause: surveyor’s donkey. I have paid the Misses Dabney one shilling and fourpence, and apologised to each in turn. The frog jug beside it bounced off the cobbles and rolled under the mangle without a mark. Whatever else may be said of the Frog Pottery, it did not skimp on the walls.

volumes.title: A Rubbing of the Frog
volumes.text:
I carried a broken yellow jug to Emberwick to be riveted, which meant Withy Bridge again and a third halfpenny. It was raining. The toll-keeper came out in her old coat, brass buttons to the chin and one odd horn one, with clay under her fingernails. I supposed she had been gardening.

Miss Philippa Quince, surveyor of Lowland jugs to the Antiquarian Society, writing from Tansy Fen. Jug No. 38, the property of the miller. Height nine inches. Here the frog is the crispest I have seen, and I took a rubbing with a soft pencil. It measures five-eighths of an inch across. It sits within a raised rim, and round it runs a border of tiny dots.

It is not cut like a potter’s seal. It looks pressed from a thing made for another purpose: a coin, or a medal. I have pinned the rubbing inside my hat.

volumes.title: Last Winter’s Jug
volumes.text:
The Antiquarian Society’s survey of Lowland jugs, kept by Miss Philippa Quince, has reached Goslingstead, and has there suffered a blow to its theory.

Jug No. 47, the property of Jem Sallow, carter. Height eight inches. Frog; thumbprint, left; clay with the sparkle in it; the wavy line beneath. Every sign of the old Frog Pottery I have been tracing since Sedgeholt. But the glaze is as bright as a new penny. I asked how long he had owned it. “Since last winter,” he said. “The floods.”

Last winter. My lost manufactory, with its chimney and its wharf, is neither lost nor, I begin to fear, a manufactory. Somebody is making these now. Somebody left-handed, near the river, who works when the water is up. I asked Jem Sallow who. He was already halfway down the lane with a load of turnips, and carters do not turn round.

volumes.title: Everybody Knows
volumes.text:
I am Miss Philippa Quince, and for eleven weeks I have surveyed the jugs of the Lowlands for the Emberwick Antiquarian Society. Of fifty-eight jugs measured, thirty-nine bear a small stamped frog. At Eelford I asked the schoolmaster, Mr Lucan Thrip, whether he had any notion who made them.

He looked at me as one looks at a child who has asked what rain is. “Dorcas Tibb,” he said. “At the toll. Everybody knows.”

It is quite simple. Lowland people are short of coin and pay the bridge toll in kind: eggs, a goose, a favour. When Mrs Tibb thinks she has had the better of the bargain, she gives a jug as change. Every road into the Lowlands crosses Withy Bridge. I have paid there three times myself. Nobody told me because I never asked. I asked only about the jugs.

volumes.title: The Sixty-Fourth Jug
volumes.text:
The survey of the jugs of the Lowlands, by Miss Philippa Quince of the Emberwick Antiquarian Society, ends where it began, at the toll-house on Withy Bridge.

Mrs Dorcas Tibb is eighty-one and left-handed. Behind the toll-house is a shed with a wheel, a kiln the size of a dog kennel, and a heap of sparkling bank clay. She makes jugs in flood winters, when the road is shut and there is nobody to charge. The frog is a brass button off her late husband’s toll coat; the wavy line is the flood. She could not see what there was to survey.

I had no halfpenny left. I paid my fourth toll with a jar of quince jam, and she judged she had the better of it. Jug No. 64. Height eight inches. Brown glaze, frog, sound. Present use: holds the Society’s pencils. Bursar carried it home without incident.

volumes.title: Packing Day
volumes.text:
Sunday, Clinker Bank. This is the diary of the Long Kiln for this year’s firing, kept by me, Odo Fenn, aged fifteen, wood-boy. Mistress Oxlade, the firing-master, gave me the book and said: write what happens, not what you feel about it. I will try.

What happened. The eleven potters of Emberwick carried their year’s work up the fell road, and we packed all three chambers, two hundred and six pots, on shelves propped with fireclay posts. It took from seven until dusk.

My gran, Nell Fenn, has a jar in the first chamber, front row, where the flame comes in hardest. She asked for that place. It is as tall as a milk churn and the last pot she will throw, because her hands have finished with clay. She set it down herself and walked home without looking back. I am not writing the rest.

volumes.title: First Smoke
volumes.text:
Monday, 6 a.m. Diary of the Long Kiln at Clinker Bank, kept by Odo Fenn, wood-boy. Lit. Mistress Oxlade, the firing-master, laid a fire the size of a hat in the mouth of the firebox and lit it with a coal I carried up from my gran’s own hearth in a tin. That is the custom when a potter has her last pot in the kiln. I did not drop it.

9 a.m. A small fire only. The pots are damp, and if the heat comes on fast the water in them turns to steam and they burst. So we warm them the way you wake somebody gently. Steam is coming off the chimney, white, smelling of wet brick.

Noon. Six barrows of larch burned. Hob Tarn, who stokes, says the first day is the dull one. He has said so four times. I think he is nervous too.

volumes.title: Night Watch
volumes.text:
Monday night, the Long Kiln, Clinker Bank. Odo Fenn’s diary. The kiln has been alight since six this morning and will burn three days without a rest, so we do not get one either.

10 p.m. The watch is me, the twins Hob and Wick Tarn, who stoke, and Mistress Oxlade, who does not seem to sleep at all. Mr Farl the baker came up with a tray of pies. He has thirty pie dishes in the first chamber and pays his share of the wood in pastry.

1 a.m. Mistress Oxlade showed me the spy-hole. You pull out a clay plug and look straight into the fire. The colour tells the heat: dull red now, like a plum. Cherry by morning, she says, then orange, then yellow, then a white you cannot look at. 3 a.m. A fox came to the edge of the light. Nineteen barrows.

volumes.title: Orange Heat
volumes.text:
Tuesday, noon. I am Odo Fenn, wood-boy at the Long Kiln above Emberwick, and this is its diary for the yearly firing. Second day. The spy-hole shows orange. We stoke every five minutes now: open the firebox door, four splits of larch, shut it, count to three hundred, again. The Tarn twins do it without speaking. I bring the barrows. Forty since Monday.

2 p.m. Lost most of my left eyebrow by looking into the firebox at the wrong moment. Wick Tarn says everyone does it once and showed me his, which never grew back properly.

4 p.m. Mistress Oxlade, the firing-master, told me to sleep on the wood-sacks in the lean-to. I said I was not tired. She said it had not been a question. Slept three hours. Dreamed I was stoking. Woke, and went and did it.

volumes.title: The Kiln Breathes
volumes.text:
Tuesday evening, Clinker Bank. The diary of the Long Kiln, written by Odo Fenn, in his first year as wood-boy.

7 p.m. Yellow heat in the first chamber. The kiln has started to breathe. Each time the twins stoke, it draws in with a low roar, and a flame a yard long stands out of the chimney top and folds back. You can see it from the town. People will be at their windows.

8 p.m. Mistress Oxlade let me have the spy-hole for a slow count of ten. My gran’s jar is in the front row, the last she will ever make. I could see it. It was not brown any longer, or any colour of clay. It was glowing clear through like a lamp, with the fire going round its shoulders like water round a stone. I was told to write what happens. That happened.

volumes.title: A Noise Inside
volumes.text:
Wednesday, 2 a.m., the Long Kiln. Odo Fenn, wood-boy, writing by the firebox light. We have been firing since Monday morning. At ten to two there was a noise inside the first chamber. A slither, then a crack, then something settling. Hob Tarn stopped with a split of larch in his hand. Nobody spoke.

Mistress Oxlade pulled the plug and looked in for a long time. Then she let me look. Something pale is leaning across the spy-hole where there was nothing before. I cannot see past it. I cannot see my gran’s jar.

“A prop’s gone,” said the firing-master. “Something has come down on something. We shall know on Monday, when she’s cold.” Then she said, “Stoke,” and they stoked. 2.30 a.m. Mr Farl the baker has gone very quiet. His pie dishes were stacked on the shelf above.

volumes.title: Nothing To Be Done
volumes.text:
Wednesday, dawn. Diary of the Long Kiln at Clinker Bank. I am Odo Fenn, and in the night something fell inside the first chamber, close to where my gran’s last jar stands.

I asked Mistress Oxlade if we could stop and open up. She did not laugh. She said the chamber is at yellow heat, and cold air on two hundred hot pots would crack every one like ice on a pond. Eleven potters’ year is in there. Whatever has happened to the jar has happened already, and stopping would only add the rest to it. “A kiln is like a pudding,” she said. “Open it early and all you learn is that you were right to worry.”

7 a.m. Sixty-eight barrows. I have decided to count wood and not think. Mr Farl the baker is counting too, on his fingers, up to thirty, over and over.

volumes.title: Test Rings
volumes.text:
Wednesday afternoon, third day of the firing at the Long Kiln. Odo Fenn, wood-boy, keeping the diary.

1 p.m. The first chamber is at white heat. Mistress Oxlade hooked a test ring out through the spy-hole on an iron rod: a small loop of glazed clay, put there to be fished for. It came out glowing and went dull, and she dropped it in the bucket and turned it to the light. The glaze had gone smooth and glassy. First chamber is done.

Now we stoke the sides. Each further chamber has its own small ports, and we post thin sticks through them, the length of a walking cane, a handful a minute. The fire climbs the hill from room to room. 5 p.m. Second chamber yellow. It is strange to feed a fire past a room you are worried about. The twins say you get used to it.

volumes.title: Rain on the Woodpile
volumes.text:
Wednesday night, Clinker Bank. Odo Fenn’s diary of the Long Kiln, third night of the firing.

11 p.m. The storm came over the fell all at once. The wind took the tarpaulin off the wood stack and the rain got in before we could catch the corners. Wet wood will not hold a kiln at white heat. For an hour the twins stoked with what was dry in the lean-to while I ran barrows, and Mr Farl went down to his bakery and came back with a cartload of his own oven faggots, which was handsome of him.

Midnight. A lantern on the fell road. My gran, who was told to stay at home, with a can of soup. She sat on an upturned barrow under the eaves and watched us stoke. She did not ask about her jar. I did not tell her about the noise. Good soup.

volumes.title: Clamming Up
volumes.text:
Thursday, 9 a.m. The Long Kiln, Clinker Bank. Diary kept by Odo Fenn, wood-boy. The last test ring came out of the third chamber glassy at ten to nine. Mistress Oxlade, the firing-master, held up her hand and the twins put down their sticks. Seventy-five hours since she lit it. One hundred and twelve barrows of wood, of which I wheeled all but nine.

Then the clamming up. We bricked the firebox mouth and smeared every door, port and crack with wet clay by the bucketful, so the heat goes out of the kiln slowly instead of in a rush. A slab went over the chimney. I plugged the spy-hole myself.

9.40 a.m. It is very quiet. There is nothing left to carry. The kiln ticks to itself as it settles. Whatever is in there is finished now, one way or the other, and sealed up.

volumes.title: Four Days
volumes.text:
Saturday. I am Odo Fenn, wood-boy, and the Long Kiln above Emberwick has been sealed and cooling since Thursday. It cannot be opened until Monday. This diary has nothing to record, so I am recording that.

I walk up to Clinker Bank each evening and lay my hand on the bricks. Thursday I could not keep it there. Friday I could, for a count of five. Today the wall is warm like a loaf.

Somewhere inside is my gran’s last jar, and whatever fell near it in the night on Wednesday. I told her about the noise in the end. She went on peeling a potato. In her first firing, she said, a whole shelf of her bowls came out welded into one lump, and she sold it to the vicar as a garden ornament. He still has it. Sunday. Warm like a cat.

volumes.title: The Opening
volumes.text:
Monday, 8 a.m. The Long Kiln, Clinker Bank. Last entry for this year’s firing, by Odo Fenn, wood-boy. Mistress Oxlade took down the door of the first chamber brick by brick. A prop had slipped. Mr Farl’s pie dishes had slid off their shelf: twenty-four whole, five in pieces, and one that had landed against the shoulder of my gran’s jar and stuck there, glazed on like a limpet.

The jar is whole. The ash has run down one side in green and gold. My gran walked round it twice. “It’s got a pocket,” she said, and laughed until she had to sit down.

It stands by her door now, holding walking sticks, with her keys in the pie dish. Mr Farl visits his dish on Sundays. Mistress Oxlade says the diary is mine again next year, and I may put one feeling in it. I am saving it.
